publisher: Export-Import Bank of the United States
title: EXIM Approves Project Vault Loan to Launch America's Strategic Critical Minerals Reserve
key_claim: The EXIM Board approved a Direct Loan of up to $10 billion to launch the US Strategic Critical Minerals Reserve, branded Project Vault, an independently governed public-private partnership storing essential raw materials across the United States to shield manufacturers from supply shocks; participating OEMs include Clarios, GE Vernova, Western Digital and Boeing.
frame_summary: EXIM argues that a public-private national reserve is needed to shield US manufacturers from supply shocks and reduce dependence on foreign-controlled supply chains.
notes: Flagship US strategic-reserve announcement; canonical primary source for the signal. Treated as the single structural anchor (Feb 2026, 3-6m band).

publisher: Center for Strategic and International Studies
title: Project Vault: A Minerals Security Backstop
key_claim: Project Vault will hold all 60 minerals on the USGS 2025 Critical Minerals List and is OEM-driven and demand-led, with manufacturers paying a commitment fee (a 'security premium') for access during disruptions rather than taxpayer subsidy; it is distinct from the 1939 National Defense Stockpile and is the largest financing in EXIM's 92-year history. In 2025, Ford halted production of its Explorer model due to a rare-earths shortage.
frame_summary: CSIS argues Project Vault is a novel demand-led economic-security backstop, distinct from a defence stockpile, that buys supply predictability without taxpayer subsidy.
notes: Tier-2 think-tank analysis of Project Vault by the director of CSIS's Critical Minerals Security Program.

title: Designing an effective strategic stockpiling system for critical minerals
date_evidence: The IEA published 'Designing an effective strategic stockpiling system for critical minerals' on January 27, 2026.
key_claim: The IEA argues that strategic stockpiles should primarily serve to ensure business continuity and provide a buffer during supply disruptions, rather than to manage price volatility or influence market dynamics, and has built a Critical Minerals Stockpiling Assessment Framework to determine which materials should be prioritised.
frame_summary: The IEA argues stockpiles should be designed for business continuity during disruptions, not price management, and prioritised by supply risk through a structured assessment framework.
notes: IEA institutional design guidance; load-bearing for the counter-argument (stockpiles should not manage prices) and the coordination thread.

publisher: Centre for Economic Transition Expertise (CETEx, LSE)
title: Dash and grab: the risks of the global race to stockpile critical minerals
key_claim: Uncoordinated unilateral stockpiling is self-defeating and may trigger the shortages it is designed to prevent; if announced programmes purchased the equivalent of 180 days of net imports, demand would exceed 10% of global annual supply for every listed commodity except nickel, creating a front-loaded shock. Cautionary precedents: the US Cold-War helium reserve (about ten times annual demand) that was liquidated cheaply and saw prices quadruple when it ran dry, and the 2022 EU gas crisis when fragmented national buying drove prices from around 20 euros to over 300 euros per MWh. The IEA is best placed to coordinate.
frame_summary: CETEx argues the answer is not to abandon reserves but to anchor them in a credible IEA-led international coordination framework, because simultaneous unilateral stockpiling amplifies the very shocks it seeks to avoid.
verbatim_quote: exceed 10% of the global annual supply of all these products except nickel
notes: LSE/CETEx commentary; analytical spine of the coordination-failure thesis. 25 March 2026, at the edge of the soft 3-month window.

title: The scramble to stockpile critical minerals could drive up energy transition costs
key_claim: New CETEx research finds that if Australia, China, the EU, India, Japan, South Korea and the US simultaneously built reserves covering six months of imports, aggregate stockpile demand could reach up to 34% of global annual cobalt supply and over 10% of global lithium, graphite and copper supply; even aggregate demand of 5% of global supply would move prices, potentially triggering the shortages and delaying the clean-energy roll-out the reserves are meant to prevent.
frame_summary: Climate Home News reports researchers warning that an uncoordinated stockpiling scramble could raise clean-energy costs and trigger the shortages it aims to prevent unless globally coordinated.
notes: Quality-journalism reporting of the June 2026 CETEx study figures plus researcher interviews.

title: Warning against 'consumer club' as G7 forms critical minerals alliance
key_claim: At the G7 leaders' summit in Evian on 17 June 2026, France, the UK, Canada, Germany, Italy, Japan, the US and the EU (with Australia) adopted a declaration to step up coordination, aggregate demand, set targets to reduce dependence on any single country outside the G7 by year-end, create a joint crisis-prevention mechanism with IEA support, build harmonised mineral-origin platforms starting with lithium and nickel, and share information on stockpiling systems; a US proposal to regulate mineral prices and a French push for a permanent secretariat failed to reach consensus. China dominates the processing of 19 of 20 critical minerals.
frame_summary: Climate Home News reports the G7 moving from national stockpiling toward a coordinated alliance (demand aggregation, crisis mechanism, information-sharing) but stopping short of binding price coordination, drawing 'consumer club' criticism.
notes: Reporting on the G7 Evian critical-minerals declaration (primary G7 PDF cited via this reporting).

title: Critical minerals geopolitics in 2026: risks, supply chains and global power shifts
date_evidence: 27 January 2026 Expert comment Written by Olena Borodyna
key_claim: US federal financing under the One Big Beautiful Bill includes about $2 billion to strengthen the critical-minerals stockpile through the National Defense Stockpile Transaction Fund, $5 billion for supply-chain investments under the Industrial Base Fund and $500 million in Defence Credit Programmes, alongside bilateral mineral deals with partners including Australia, the DRC, Japan, Malaysia, Thailand and Ukraine; China is projected to supply around 80% of battery-grade graphite and rare earths by 2035.
frame_summary: ODI argues 2026 critical-minerals competition is defined by US bilateral and state-backed financing, EU financing gaps, and China's enduring processing dominance under its 15th Five-Year Plan.
notes: Tier-2 think-tank framing of the wider 2026 critical-minerals policy landscape and US stockpile funding.
